subject: [PATCH v2] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch does not handle misaligned copies of size 512 to 640 bytes correctly, which were slower than the scalar loop in v1, and requested raising the threshold from 512 to 2048 bytes.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the patch's assumption that REP MOVSB would always improve performance on ERMS CPUs, citing specific alignment issues on Zen and Intel CPUs, including a case where REP MOVSB is slower due to misalignment between source and destination buffers.
reviews.raw_body:
On Wed,  4 Nov 2026 14:28:06 -0800
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

Which cpu type was that?
Do I remember the older zen cpu falling back to byte copies?
I wonder if it is possibly to do a run-time patch of the constant.
In all the tests I've done on Intel cpu (going back to sandy bridge)
the only alignment that made any difference was 64 byte (32 on older cpu)
alignment of the destination buffer.

That could be 'for further study'.

There are some very bad alignment pairs on some cpu.
On zen5 if (IIRC) (src - dest) % PAGE_SIZE is between 1 and 127 then
the both setup and per-byte cost of REP MOSVB are significantly higher
(the byte alignment makes minimal difference throughout).
I don't remember finding anything similar on the Intel cpu I tested.
But it is probably not worth checking for them because the cost of the
comparison will be larger overall.

David

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary:
The author addressed a concern about the patch's applicability to specific CPU models by confirming that Zen 1 and Zen 2 do not have ERMS or FSRM, thus keeping the scalar loop, while Zen 3 onwards use REP MOVSB for every size.

Author acknowledges that using REP MOVSB for small copies might be beneficial but wants to prioritize the current usecase-driven approach from zstd/btrfs.

The author clarifies that the performance issue with REP MOVSB on misaligned copies between 512 and 640 bytes was due to specific alignment, not a general problem with using REP MOVSB at this threshold.

Author agrees that the current patch is acceptable, but suggests investigating further if a use case for smaller sizes can be found.
reviews.raw_body:
I just checked, and Zen 1 and Zen 2 have neither ERMS nor FSRM, so
they keep the scalar loop. Zen 3 onwards has both, and FSRM already
uses REP MOVSB for every size.

---

It might be possible. But I wanted to keep the patch usecase driven.
The current usecase is coming from zstd/btrfs. If we find a usecase
where it might be faster for smaller copies, it might become worth
looking into then?

---

Also I should have been clearer in the changelog, by "misaligned copies of
512 to 640 bytes", I had tested a 513-byte copy with the source at page offset
1 and destination at 63, it took on average 62 ns with REP MOVSB versus
49 ns with scalar. I had done a couple of other tests at 640 bytes as well.

---

Yes, I agree.

Do you think this version of the patch seems acceptable?

I feel like we should only investigate for lower size if we can find a
usecase.

2026-11-05.patch_summary: This patch optimizes large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM by using the REP MOVSB instruction from 2048 bytes onwards, reducing execution time by up to 66.8%. The patch also folds memcpy_orig() into __memcpy() and makes adjustments for FSRM CPUs. Smaller copies continue to use a scalar loop for performance reasons.

The patch also folds memcpy_orig() into __memcpy() and makes adjustments for FSRM CPUs. Smaller copies continue to use a scalar loop for performance reasons.

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Kiryl Shutsemau questioned whether any RET in a replacement needs to be aligned, and suggested comparing Linus' layout which keeps the RET out of the replacement, potentially avoiding an ITS problem.

Reviewer noted that the RCX/RDX swap in the patch only saves one MOV on copies of 2K and up, and suggested an alternative implementation to replace the swap with a conditional jump based on ERMS feature
reviews.raw_body:
Does this mean any RET in a replacement needs the same alignment? Would
anything catch it if the next one doesn't have it?

Linus' layout keeps the RET out of the replacement, with no padding:

	movq %rdi, %rax
	movq %rdx, %rcx
	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "rep movsb", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
	RET

Non-FSRM takes the same jump it takes today. Does that avoid the ITS
problem? Why not this layout?

---

The RCX/RDX swap is most of the diff, and all it saves is one MOV on
copies of 2K and up.

What about something like this? Untested.

diff --git a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
--- a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
+++ b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
@@ -31,11 +31,9 @@
  * which the compiler could/should do much better anyway.
  */
 SYM_TYPED_FUNC_START(__memcpy)
-	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
-
 	movq %rdi, %rax
 	movq %rdx, %rcx
-	rep movsb
+	ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "rep movsb", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
 	RET
 SYM_FUNC_END(__memcpy)
 EXPORT_SYMBOL(__memcpy)
@@ -45,11 +43,11 @@ SYM_PIC_ALIAS(memcpy)
 EXPORT_SYMBOL(memcpy)

 SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
-	movq %rdi, %rax
-
 	cmpq $0x20, %rdx
 	jb .Lhandle_tail

+	ALTERNATIVE "", __stringify(shrq $11, %rcx; jnz .Lerms), X86_FEATURE_ERMS
+
 	/*
 	 * We check whether memory false dependence could occur,
 	 * then jump to corresponding copy mode.
@@ -169,5 +167,10 @@ SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)

 .Lend:
 	RET
+
+.Lerms:
+	movq %rdx, %rcx
+	rep movsb
+	RET
 SYM_FUNC_END(memcpy_orig)

If you keep the swap, please make it a separate patch with no functional
change.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch does not handle the case where the length is a power of two, which can result in slower performance due to the shift operation used for ERMS CPUs.

Reviewer David Laight expressed concern about the alignment of the FSRM replacement, suggesting it should be aligned to avoid performance issues when the RET instruction is in the first half of a cache line.

The reviewer expressed concern about the added jump instruction on non-FSRM CPUs, suggesting it could have a measurable impact on performance in cold cache scenarios, but noted that this would only be an issue if RET is not always 0xc3.

Reviewer David Laight suggested that the patch could be improved by avoiding unnecessary register-register moves and instead using a simple backtrack to get the value where it is needed, criticizing GCC for being bad at this optimization.
sentiment_signals: compiler really ought to do a lot better
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:25:54 +0000
Kiryl Shutsemau <kas@kernel.org> wrote:

---

My suspicion is that ideally 'yes'.
But someone said (in this thread) that it is worse for RET in the first
half a cache line - so aligning the replacement that way is better.)

---

It adds a jump to the non-FSRM path.
Cold cache that is likely to be measurable.
(But not if RET ends up being anything other than 0xc3 -  that will
just kill everything.)

---

Register-register moves don't cost much (they can even be done my the
register renaming logic rather than the alu - but still have to be
fetched and decoded), but needing them is a bit of 'lack of attention
detail' when a simple backtrack can get the value where it is needed.
gcc is very bad at it, a compiler really ought to do a lot better.

David

reviews.author: Linus Torvalds
reviews.summary: Reviewer Linus Torvalds strongly disagrees with the patch, citing concerns about the use of 'RET' in assembly code alternatives, which he believes is a bad practice.
reviews.raw_body:
Let's not do that.

Putting magic things like RET in alternatives is just a bad bad idea.

               Linus

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the ERMS check should be done after the 32-byte check to avoid unnecessary reloads, and suggested keeping the count in RCX for REP MOVSB

Reviewer David Laight suggested that the RET instruction in the FSRM replacement should be left in the code and then overwritten, expressing concern about the functionality of the code patching process.
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:53:07 -0800
Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org> wrote:

---

You'd definitely want the RET in the code itself, and then overwrite
it with something else.
When I suggested it I did wonder whether the code patching really had
the right functionality.

Someone should try to measure it [1], but I actually suspect that the only
cost in following a 'rep movs' with an unconditional 'jmp' would be
for an I-cache load (or, worse, a TLB miss).
I expect the pipeline front end (which handles the jmp) will do all its
work while the setup for rep movs is happening (even for FSRM).

That would mean you could pair the "cmpq $0x20, %rcx; jb .Lhandle_tail"
with "rep movsb; jmps do_RET; nop".

David

[1] I need to dig out my 'rep movs' performance measuring code and run
it on a few different cpu types.
But I not got anything newer than an i7-7 or a zen[1-4].

reviews.author: H. Anvin
reviews.summary: Reviewer H. Anvin questioned the use of REP MOVSB in assembly code, suggesting that it's a bad practice due to potential portability issues.
reviews.raw_body:
Why is that, *given that it is in assembly*?

For C (or Rust, or C++, ...) it is obviously bad chicken.

reviews.author: Linus Torvalds
reviews.summary: Reviewer Linus Torvalds expressed concerns about the use of magic in assembly code, specifically in the alternatives section, and suggested avoiding it to prevent issues with relocations. He noted that a similar pattern is already used in memmove_64.S but acknowledged that it's not ideal.
sentiment_signals: concerns about magic in assembly code
reviews.raw_body:
It's assembly, but it's assembly that potentially gets rewritten.
objtool already knows about __x86_return_thunk being special (although
I think it's the _target_, not the call site, it cares about).

I would like to not have magic in stuff that is in the alternatives
section. We've had issues with relocations etc before.

That said, grepping a bit for this, it turns out we already seem to be
doing that in memmove_64.S, although it was hidden from my first grep:

  #define CHECK_LEN     cmp $0x20, %rdx; jb 1f
  #define MEMMOVE_BYTES movq %rdx, %rcx; rep movsb; RET
  .Lmemmove_begin_forward:
        ALTERNATIVE_2 __stringify(CHECK_LEN), \
                      __stringify(CHECK_LEN; MEMMOVE_BYTES), X86_FEATURE_ERMS, \
                      __stringify(MEMMOVE_BYTES), X86_FEATURE_FSRM

which is pretty disgusting. But I guess that train has passed..

           Linus

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch does not handle the case where the length is a power of two, which can cause REP MOVSB to be slower than the scalar loop.

Reviewer David Laight expressed concern about using RET in the FSRM replacement due to its potential for multiple speculative execution issues, suggesting that if it were just a single opcode byte (0xc3), it wouldn't be an issue.
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:17:51 -0800
"H. Peter Anvin" <hpa@zytor.com> wrote:

---

Because RET is a horrid sequence subject to a lot of patching
to avoid multiple speculative execution issues.
If is were just the 0xc3 opcode byte it wouldn't be an issue.

David

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch's ERMS check should be done after the 32-byte check, so copies below 32 bytes skip it, and suggested keeping the count in RCX to avoid reloading for REP MOVSB.

Reviewer David Laight pointed out that on ERMS CPUs, the RET instruction in the FSRM replacement is likely to be a 5-byte JMP instruction, which would cause issues when checking for replacement by (0xcc)*4 due to misaligned addresses.
reviews.raw_body:
On Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:59:02 -0800
Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org> wrote:

---

Or no one has realised it ran straight through the buffers :-)
RET is likely to be a 5 byte jmp instruction.
One of the checks for letting it be replaced by 0xc3,(0xcc)*4 is (addr & 0x20).
That will be wrong for the alternatives (half the time) so a quarter
of the time the train will go straight through the buffers.

David

The patch also folds memcpy_orig() into __memcpy() and makes adjustments for FSRM CPUs. Smaller copies continue to use a scalar loop for performance reasons.
